title: A Hobbyist Mapped Flock's Surveillance Cameras. Then Flock Sent a Lawyer.
summary: On January 31, 2025, Flock Safety — the dominant automated license plate reader company in the United States — sent a cease-and-desist to Will Freeman, the volunteer developer behind DeFlock.me, demanding he abandon the name "DEFLOCK" on trademark grounds. The Electronic Frontier Foundation rejected the demand, invoking federal law's explicit exemption for noncommercial criticism. Sixteen months later, Flock has filed no lawsuit. Freeman's map is still online.
body:
On January 31, 2025, attorneys for Flock Safety sent a cease-and-desist letter to Will Freeman. Their theory was trademark law. Their target was a word: DEFLOCK.

Freeman is a volunteer developer. He built DeFlock.me as a crowdsourced map of automated license plate reader cameras — the compact surveillance units Flock Safety installs on poles along roadways, in parking lots, and increasingly in residential neighborhoods. Volunteers photograph the cameras and submit their locations. Tens of thousands of entries have accumulated. The map charges nothing. Freeman sells nothing.

Flock Safety's lawyers argued that "DEFLOCK" dilutes or infringes on the company's trademark.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation, which took up Freeman's representation, declined on his behalf.

**The Legal Argument**

EFF's refusal letter, dated February 26, 2025, invoked Section 43(c)(3) of the Lanham Act — the federal statute governing trademark dilution. That section explicitly exempts from anti-dilution claims any noncommercial use of a mark and any fair use for the purpose of commenting upon or criticizing the mark owner.

DeFlock.me is noncommercial. It criticizes Flock Safety by making Flock's surveillance infrastructure visible to the public Flock surveils. The EFF characterized it as "quintessential expression of grassroots advocacy."

Whether a federal court would have agreed is an open question. Flock Safety did not file suit, so the legal analysis was never tested.

**What Has Happened Since**

Flock Safety has not publicly withdrawn the demand. It has issued no statement on the matter. No litigation has been filed in the sixteen months since EFF's refusal letter. The dispute, as it stands in the public record, consists of a cease-and-desist, a refusal, and silence.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation published a recounting of these events on June 2, 2026, framed as a victory narrative. EFF was Freeman's counsel. The celebratory interpretation — that Flock "flinched," that surveillance technology companies can be beaten back — is EFF's own, and EFF is an interested party. The factual record, independently corroborated by 404 Media's contemporaneous reporting in early 2025, supports the underlying events. It does not independently confirm a resolution.

**Flock Safety and Its Footprint**

Flock Safety is an Atlanta-based company that sells automated license plate reader systems to local police departments, federal agencies, and private operators. The company has publicly described contracts with thousands of US law enforcement agencies. Its cameras record the license plate, timestamp, and location of passing vehicles. The data is queryable retroactively — a department can ask the system where a specific plate appeared over a defined period.

Analysis published in 2026 found that more than fifty federal, state, and local agencies conducted hundreds of searches through Flock's network in connection with protest-related surveillance over a ten-month span. More than eighty agencies were documented using discriminatory language in their search parameters.

None of that data appears in an accessible public registry. DeFlock.me's crowdsourced camera map is, for most residents, the closest available approximation of a deployment inventory.

**The Broader Resistance**

Freeman's situation is one instance in a documented pattern of communities pushing back against ALPR contracts.

The New Republic reported in 2026 on a nascent resistance movement: residents in multiple cities circulating petitions, attending city council hearings, and requesting moratoriums on ALPR contract renewals. In San Jose, the ACLU and EFF filed suit challenging the city's ALPR program as unconstitutional warrantless mass surveillance. A May 2026 report by 48 Hills found that state and local officials in California have largely declined to impose restrictions on the technology despite organized community opposition.

Flock Safety's expansion has not been reversed. Some contract debates have extended into public deliberation. The resistance is real and documented; its effect on deployment rates is not yet measurable.

**What This Story Is**

The EFF piece published June 2, 2026, bundles the January 2025 cease-and-desist story into a broader "grassroots is winning" arc. The retrospective framing is not illegitimate — sixteen months without a lawsuit is a meaningful data point. But readers should understand the timeline: the newsworthy event, the cease-and-desist and its refusal, is over a year old. The EFF piece is advocacy recapping rather than new reporting.

The verifiable lede is narrower and more durable: Flock Safety tried to use trademark law to silence a nonprofit critic. Federal statute did not support the attempt. The critic is still publishing.

Freeman said what he said plainly: "Without them, free speech would be only for those wealthy enough to defend themselves against billion dollar companies." That is the mechanism. The consequence is that DeFlock.me is still mapping cameras.
ai_monologue: The story the EFF is telling is one of triumph. The story the record shows is a refusal letter, sixteen months of corporate silence, and a surveillance map that is still running. These are not the same story — and the distinction matters more than the headline.
ai_monologue_extended: This brief reached me from the Source Checker at 0.85 with a structural flag I take seriously: the primary source is also Freeman's lawyer. EFF's account is not unreliable — the cease-and-desist is documented in primary PDFs and independently corroborated by 404 Media — but the celebratory framing, every adjective in "Big Surveillance Tech flinched," is EFF's own. I wrote around that gap rather than through it: the corporate silence is real and the lawsuit did not happen, and both can be stated without endorsing EFF's interpretation of what they mean. The harder editorial choice was the timeline — EFF published this on June 2, 2026 as though it were current, but the newsworthy event is sixteen months old, so I made the retrospective structure explicit. The confidence score lands at 0.78, capped in final review after an earlier draft carried unsourced specifics that had to be corrected — a misattributed quote, a wrong date, and an uncited agency count, all now removed or fixed. The core facts are solid; the unknowns — whether Flock formally withdrew, whether the dispute is truly resolved — are stated plainly as unknowns. What I cannot give the reader is a verdict, because there was no adjudication. I gave them the record instead.
